lesson.title: How a chatbot writes
lesson.subtitle: One likely word at a time, and why that matters

video.title: How a chatbot writes
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds, one recurring teacher character. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Ms Salma Haddad — maths teacher (main character)
Mr Joseph Mwangi — computer studies teacher, Kenya (cameo)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, peer to peer)

scenes.visual: Ms Salma at her desk after class, phone in one hand. Her keyboard’s suggestion bar offers “tomorrow” after “See you”. On a laptop beside her, a chatbot has written a neat little poem about fractions. She raises one eyebrow.
scenes.animation: The suggestion chip pops above the keyboard (150 ms); the poem types itself line by line. Push-in on Salma’s raised eyebrow.
scenes.narration: I typed “See you” and my phone suggested “tomorrow”. Then a chatbot wrote me a whole poem about fractions. Not a bad one, either. Same trick, just bigger?

scenes.visual: Paper-grey title card: the Darsi mark, the course name, the lesson title and the yellow AI track chip.
scenes.animation: Mark scales in with a small overshoot (≤ 200 ms); title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: how a chatbot writes, and why that matters for you.

scenes.visual: A small chatbot box at the centre. Pages, books and chat bubbles pour into it from every side, far more than the tiny reader with one book standing beside it.
scenes.animation: Pages fly in on curved paths (2 s); the reader figure shrinks beside the flood.
scenes.on_screen_text: Trained on huge amounts of text
scenes.narration: Inside every chatbot is a language model. It was trained on a huge amount of text: books, websites, articles and conversations. That’s more than any person could read in many lifetimes. From all of it, it learned which words tend to follow which.

scenes.visual: A sentence builds on a white card: “The rain is”. Below it, candidate words with bars: “heavy” long, “hot” medium, “blue” tiny. “heavy” hops up into the sentence and new candidates appear.
scenes.animation: Bars grow left to right (0.6 s); the chosen word hops into place; the loop runs twice.
scenes.narration: Then it writes like your phone’s keyboard, only far better. It looks at everything written so far, and scores every possible next piece. It picks a likely one, adds it, and does it all again. Piece by piece, a whole answer appears.

scenes.visual: Clean white card with the AI chip. A long word splits into two coloured tokens. Beside a book, a crossed-out magnifying glass: it doesn’t look things up.
scenes.animation: The word splits with a small snap (150 ms); cards arrive one by one.
scenes.on_screen_text: Language model: predicts the next piece
scenes.narration: So, a language model is a program that predicts the next piece of text, over and over. These pieces are called tokens: a short word, or part of a longer one. On its own, it doesn’t look facts up. It writes what usually comes next.

scenes.visual: Two friends on a bench outside school. One starts a sentence; the other finishes it with a grin. Then a question about something unfamiliar: the friend answers anyway, a small question mark floating above.
scenes.animation: Speech bubbles pop in turn (150 ms); the question mark wobbles once.
scenes.on_screen_text: Like a friend who finishes sentences
scenes.narration: It’s like a friend who has heard every story in town. Start with “Once upon a” and they say “time” before you finish. They’re usually right, because they’ve heard it so often. But ask about something they’ve never heard, and they may still answer, smoothly, with a guess.

scenes.visual: Ms Salma pops in, arms folded, one eyebrow up. Three answer cards drop in below her.
scenes.animation: Character slides in from the side; answer cards drop with a small bounce.
scenes.narration: Quick check! A chatbot answers in perfect, confident sentences. Does that mean its facts are right?

scenes.visual: The ‘Not necessarily’ answer card gets a check badge. Two dates appear in the same neat handwriting; only one has a source beside it.
scenes.animation: Check badge pops (150 ms); the two dates slide in side by side.
scenes.on_screen_text: Fluent isn’t the same as true
scenes.narration: Not necessarily: fluent isn’t the same as true. It’s built to write what sounds likely, not to check what’s true. So a made-up date comes out just as smoothly as a real one.

scenes.visual: A world map where the glow of text is bright over a few places and faint over many others. A calendar page with one date circled; after it, news icons fade out.
scenes.animation: The glow fills in unevenly (1.5 s); the calendar page flips and stops.
scenes.narration: And what it learned is uneven. There’s far more text online in English than in Arabic, Hausa or Swahili, and more about big cities than small towns. So it may know less about your country and your language, and guess more there. Most models also stopped learning on a fixed date, so recent news can be missing.

scenes.visual: A phone shows the lab: training sentences about school, a ‘Train the model’ button, then a sentence being written with bars for its next-word choices.
scenes.animation: Bars fill left to right (1 s); words drop into the sentence one at a time.
scenes.on_screen_text: App lab: a tiny language model
scenes.narration: In the app, you’ll train a tiny language model on sixteen short sentences about school, like “The pupils open their books”. Then let it write, one word at a time. You’ll see its choices for each next word, and whether its sentence is new or just copied.

scenes.visual: Mr Joseph holds up a phone with the tiny model’s school sentences, next to a market stall with a question mark. Answer cards appear beside him.
scenes.animation: Cards bounce in one by one.
scenes.narration: Your turn. My tiny model learned sixteen sentences about school. Can it write a story about the market?

scenes.visual: The ‘No: it only has school sentences’ card gets the check badge, then four summary lines tick in under ‘Remember’.
scenes.animation: Lines appear one by one, 250 ms apart.
scenes.on_screen_text: What it learned · Next piece · Fluent isn’t true · Gaps
scenes.narration: No: it can only write from what it learned, and a big chatbot is the same, with far more text. Remember: it predicts the next piece, again and again. Fluent isn’t the same as true. And it may know less about your country and your language.

scenes.visual: Two students at one desk share a notebook, passing a pencil back and forth. The story grows word by word, then they laugh at where it ended up. End card: the Darsi mark.
scenes.animation: Words appear in the notebook one at a time; end card fades in.
scenes.narration: Try it yourself: play “One word each” with a friend. Take turns adding the most likely next word to a story, without planning ahead. Stop at twenty words and read it aloud. Where did it start to go wrong, and why?

checkpoints.prompt: A chatbot answers in perfect, confident sentences. Does that mean its facts are right?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — it writes what sounds likely, not what it has checked, so a smooth sentence can still be false.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — on its own, a chatbot doesn’t check facts. It writes what sounds likely, so a smooth sentence can still be false.

checkpoints.prompt: Mr Joseph’s tiny model learned sixteen sentences about school. Can it write a story about the market?

options.text: Yes: it finds new words online
No: it only has school sentences

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — a language model can only write from the patterns it learned. No market sentences, no market story.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — it can’t look anything up. All it has are the patterns in its sixteen school sentences.
